rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing retained compounds. The intermediate temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction.

Halve the gradient slope while keeping temperature and endpoints fixed to measure which crowded pairs respond to slope. This should also reveal whether the late doublet needs temperature-based selectivity tuning.
The shallower gradient resolved most of the cluster but left one close pair. Raising temperature tests selectivity for that pair while aiming to bring the last peak below 10 minutes.
Test the midpoint temperature to separate the new co-elution at 60 C while retaining the selectivity improvement over 40 C. Keeping the gradient fixed isolates the temperature effect.
At 60 C only one pair remains unresolved, so test a moderately steeper gradient to move away from its co-elution condition. This also creates more time margin below 10 minutes.

Further steepening should improve the remaining close pair, whose resolution increased strongly from 24 to 20 minutes. The neighboring pairs will be checked for loss of resolution as the run shortens.

Keep the successful gradient slope of injection 6 while shifting the starting composition slightly higher. This tests whether the small selectivity change can lift the marginal R = 1.46 pair above 1.5 without sacrificing the other pairs.

Slightly reduce the slope from injection 7 to improve both early close pairs while using its extra resolution margin in the later pair. The endpoint remains well above the observed elution window, and the last peak should stay below 10 minutes.

Reduce the slope slightly further to 0.045 organic fraction per minute, targeting full resolution of both marginal early pairs while preserving the later pair’s remaining margin. The final composition is above the last peak’s estimated elution composition.

Injection 9 has reached the maximum CRF and remains the benchmark. Test a higher starting composition with a slightly shallower slope to shorten retention while attempting to preserve the three marginal separations.

Return to the fully resolved starting composition and increase slope only slightly, from 0.045 to 0.04583 per minute. This tests whether retention can be shortened without dropping either early critical pair below R = 1.5; injection 9 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Injection 9 already achieves the maximum score, and local steepening has begun sacrificing resolution. Explore lower-temperature selectivity with the original fast scouting gradient to look for a different, potentially shorter fully resolved method.

Test a shallower gradient at 25 C to determine whether both remaining close pairs improve with slope. This characterizes the promising low-temperature selectivity before trimming the starting composition to shorten retention.

Test a modest temperature increase to shift the stubborn central pair away from co-elution, retaining the slope of injection 13. Raising the starting composition trims unused gradient space and should shorten the run substantially.

Reduce the slope at the promising trimmed, low-temperature condition to move the central pair through its apparent selectivity crossover. The other pairs have resolution margin, and the last peak should remain below 10 minutes.

Raise temperature one step while holding the gradient fixed to shift the remaining early co-elution. Monitor the late pair closely because temperature may improve the early pair at the expense of late selectivity.

Test the cooler side of injection 15’s early-pair crossover, where separation may recover without creating the central co-elution seen at 35 C. The last peak is expected to remain below 10 minutes, with injection 9 retained as the maximum-score benchmark.

Raise the starting composition while preserving injection 17’s gradient slope to remove time spent below the elution window. This tests whether the fully resolved low-temperature method can approach the speed of injection 9 without losing its critical separations.

Test beyond the central-pair crossover induced by raising the starting composition, keeping the slope fixed. Separation may recover on the other side while shortening retention further; check that the first peak remains retained and all other pairs stay resolved.

Injection 19 is fully resolved and substantially faster than the earlier maximum-score methods. Shorten its gradient by one grid step to reduce retention while testing the resolution margin in the central and late pairs.

Shorten the gradient one more step to locate the speed limit of this fully resolved region. The central pair at R = 1.85 is likely to become limiting; injection 20 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.
Back off the slope to a value between injections 20 and 21 by lowering the endpoint one step. This should restore the marginal central pair above R = 1.5 while remaining faster than injection 20.

Raise temperature one step to test whether this fully resolved method can run faster while retaining its selectivity. Injection 22 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method if any pair falls below R = 1.5.

Return to 25 C and test a higher starting composition with a shallower gradient to offset compression of the critical central pair. This explores another route to faster full resolution while retaining injection 22 as the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Trim injection 22’s gradient endpoint while preserving its starting composition, temperature, and slope; the last peak’s estimated elution composition is approximately 0.525. This should retain full resolution and the approximately 4.14-minute last peak while completing the programmed gradient in 4 rather than 8 minutes.
